summary: globMatch checks the literal/`?` arm BEFORE the `*` arm, so a `*` in the pattern that lines up with a literal `*` in the value is consumed as a literal and never registered as a backtrack point. The matcher then contradicts its own docstring ("`*` = any run (including empty)").
failure: matchGlob('*', '*ops') === false (must be true); matchGlob('a*', 'a*b') === false; filterHandles([{handle:'*ops'}], '*') === [] . Reproduced: a length<=4 corpus over the alphabet {a,*,?} on BOTH sides yields 546 pattern x value disagreements against the exhaustive reference matcher already present in identity-filter.test.ts. Reachable via parley_list_users({filter:'*'}): a peer whose identity.handle contains '*' (config only requires min length 1) is silently dropped from a glob-filtered roster, i.e. it reads as unreachable.
remediation: Swap the two arms of the loop so `pattern[p] === '*'` is tested first: `if (p < P && pattern[p] === '*') { lastStar = p; starEnd = s; p++; } else if (p < P && (pattern[p] === '?' || pattern[p] === value[s])) { p++; s++; }`. Verified in the worktree: the one-line reorder drives all 546 disagreements to zero and leaves identity-filter.test.ts and stated-bounds.test.ts green.
testUpgrade: The class is "a metacharacter appearing as a LITERAL in the matched value". The existing exhaustive-reference test is the right instrument but its VALUES alphabet is ['a','b'] and so can never contain '*' or '?'. Widen the generator to words(['a','b','*','?'], 4) on the value side as well as the pattern side (and keep the pattern side at ['a','b','*','?']); assert zero disagreements with referenceMatch over the full cross product. Add the same widening to the hand table rows (['*','*a',true], ['a*','a*b',true], ['*','**',true]) so a failure names the shape.

summary: `allowlistFor` is the single function that turns a ParleyConfig into the runtime security boundary (it is what every composition root calls), and NO test exercises it. Two independent mutations to it leave the entire bridge-core suite green.
failure: Mutation 1: delete `reserved: [cfg.presence.topic]`. Result: 38 files / 1873 tests PASS. With that line gone, a config carrying `post_topics: ['.*']` makes `parley_post({topic:'parley-presence', content:'{"kind":"hello",...}'})` succeed, so any caller — or a prompt-injected agent acting on untrusted inbound content — can forge presence beats and spoof the parley_list_users roster; the class docstring's promise that "a peer cannot spoof the presence roster" silently stops holding. Mutation 2: `new Allowlist([...cfg.topics, ...cfg.post_topics], {...})`. Result: 1873 tests PASS, even though it puts raw regex sources into the EXPLICIT set that subscribe/catch-up/presence iterate — exactly the "patterns never widen subscribe" invariant the docstring states. Allowlist's own class-level tests pass `reserved`/`postPatterns` by hand and therefore cannot see either.
remediation: Add a test module for `allowlistFor` that drives it from parseConfig output only: (a) with `post_topics: ['.*']`, assert `has(cfg.presence.topic) === false` and `assert(presenceTopic)` throws TopicNotAllowedError; (b) assert `topics()` equals `cfg.topics` exactly (no pattern source leaks in) for a config with several post_topics; (c) assert a pattern-matched topic is `has`-true but absent from `topics()`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "config -> boundary wiring" rather than these two lines: build a table of configs (no patterns / one pattern / broad `.*` / custom presence.topic / presence.enabled false) and for each assert the three-way partition as a property — every topic in `cfg.topics` is in `topics()`; `topics()` contains nothing that is not in `cfg.topics`; `has(cfg.presence.topic)` is false under every row including the broad-pattern and presence-disabled rows. A row generated from the config object means a future config field (a second reserved topic, a `subscribe_topics` list) is graded the moment it appears.

summary: The full-match anchoring `^(?:src)$` is a stated security property (the docstring and CLAUDE.md's security lens both name "anchored post_topics"), but no test distinguishes it from `^src$`. Dropping the non-capturing group survives the whole suite.
failure: Mutation: `return new RegExp(`^${src}$`)`. Result: 38 files / 1873 tests PASS. Under that mutation `post_topics: ['ops|dev']` compiles to /^ops|dev$/, so `has('secret-dev')` is true and `has('ops-anything')` is true — a config line that reads as two narrow topics mints a post/fetch set reaching arbitrary topics. Nothing notices because neither allowlist.test.ts's SAFE table nor testing/regex-corpus.ts contains a single source with a TOP-LEVEL bare alternation: every alternation in both is already wrapped in its own group ('(alpha|beta)-.*', '(?:ops|dev|qa)-[a-z]+'), which is precisely the shape the wrapper is redundant for.
remediation: Add sources whose meaning changes under re-association to the shared corpus and assert the negative: `new Allowlist(['ctx'], { postPatterns: ['ops|dev'] })` must have `has('secret-dev') === false`, `has('ops-x') === false`, `has('ops') === true`, `has('dev') === true`. Apply the same rows to presence.ts's compilePeerPatterns, which wraps identically.
testUpgrade: Parameterize on the class "source whose top level is an alternation or an anchor": table of [src, mustMatch[], mustNotMatch[]] with rows 'ops|dev', 'a|b|c', '^ops', 'ops$', '|ops', 'ops|', '.*|x' — driven through all three entry points already enumerated in regex-screen-parity.test.ts (isRedosSafeSource is exempt; Allowlist and parseConfig+allowlistFor are not). A row asserting only "the listed topic matches" cannot fail; the mustNotMatch column is what pins the anchoring.

summary: seam.ts is the canonical contract a plugin author reads, and its fetchRecent JSDoc states the SQLite reference backend returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '0' }` for a never-posted topic. It does not, and has not since cursors became store-scoped.
failure: packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:231 returns `nextCursor: last?.cursor ?? mintCursor(storeId, resumeAfter ?? 0n)` and mintCursor (line 500) is `asCursor(`${storeId}.${rowid}`)`, so the empty-topic cursor is e.g. '9f3a1c2b.0' — never '0'. A plugin author following the doc literally emits '0', which sqlite's own resume path documents (index.ts:236) as "another backend's numeric cursor reaching this plugin" and treats as a foreign store.
remediation: Drop the parenthetical value or restate it structurally: "the SQLite reference backend returns an empty page whose nextCursor encodes its store id and rowid 0". The load-bearing part of the contract is replayability, not the literal.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a seam doc quoting a concrete backend value" mechanically rather than by re-reading prose: the conformance suite already asserts replayability at packages/conformance/src/index.ts:241; extend the same case to assert `first.nextCursor` is a non-empty string AND that `String(first.nextCursor)` round-trips as `since` — then delete every literal cursor value from seam.ts's prose so there is nothing left to rot. A source-lint row (in the existing source-hygiene.test.ts style) banning a quoted cursor literal in seam.ts JSDoc would pin it durably.

summary: `isDisambiguated` returns false when `name.length === sep.length + hashLen`, which is exactly the length of a minted name whose sanitized prefix is empty. So the pass-through branch and the disambiguating branch are NOT disjoint at that boundary, and safeName — documented as an unqualified "injective topic -> backend-name mapping" for any caller-supplied fold — collides.
failure: With `sanitize = s => s.replace(/[^a-z0-9-]/g,'')` (a charset fold that DELETES rather than replaces, a natural third-party shape): safeName(asTopic('  ')) === '-099600a10a' (sanitized is '', so the minted name is sep+hash, length 11), and safeName(asTopic('-099600a10a')) === '-099600a10a' (pass-through, because isDisambiguated's `<=` refuses to recognise a length-11 name). Two distinct topics land on one backend channel and cross-deliver; an attacker who can choose a topic can compute the target name. Reproduced in the worktree. No shipped fold is affected today — all five (sanitizeAlias/Token/Name/Local/Nick) replace rather than delete — so this is a latent hole in exported public API.
remediation: Change the guard to `if (name.length < sep.length + hashLen) return false;`. Optionally also refuse a fold that maps a non-empty topic to the empty string, which is the only way to reach the boundary.
testUpgrade: The existing closure test (topic-name.test.ts:186) is the right instrument but its `folds` table contains only total-replacement folds, so no fold can ever produce an empty sanitized form and the boundary is unreachable. Add a deleting fold (`s => s.replace(/[^a-z0-9-]/g,'')`) and a lowercasing+deleting fold to the shared `folds` table so all four generated describes (closure-injectivity, fixed-point, near-miss, COLLAPSED corpus) grade them; add SEEDS that fold to '' ('  ', '!!!', ' ') plus the minted names of those seeds. That guards the CLASS "pass-through and disambiguated branches must be disjoint at every length", not just this one length.

summary: MAX_AMBIGUITY is documented as the backtracking bound and calibrated so "the worst accepted source finishes in single-digit milliseconds", but it is a PER-SOURCE bound. `post_topics` has no `.max()` on the array and `Allowlist.has` runs `.some()` over every compiled pattern, so the calibrated cost multiplies by an unbounded count.
failure: Measured in the worktree: `post_topics` filled with N copies of the worst source the screen accepts at the bound — '[ab]?'.repeat(16) + 'a'.repeat(16) + 'z<i>' (96 chars, budget exactly 2^16 = MAX_AMBIGUITY, 2.7ms alone) — blocks the event loop inside ONE `allow.has('a'.repeat(64))` call for 260ms at N=100, 2.6s at N=1000 and 19.0s at N=5000. Every parley_post / parley_reply / parley_fetch_recent call pays it, and config.test.ts:493 states this repo's own threat model that a config file "is not always operator-authored end to end — generated, templated, or committed by someone else". engine/presence.ts already caps the analogous untrusted list at MAX_RECORD_TOPICS = 64; the operator-side list is uncapped, so the two paths disagree about whether the budget composes.
remediation: Put a `.max()` on `post_topics` in ConfigSchema (a count that keeps count x MAX_AMBIGUITY inside the same single-digit-millisecond envelope the constant is calibrated to — 64 mirrors MAX_RECORD_TOPICS) and amend the MAX_AMBIGUITY docstring to say the bound is per source and that callers must also bound HOW MANY sources they match against one input.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "aggregate cost across a screened collection" rather than one pattern shape: a parameterized budget test that, for each entry point compiling unauthored patterns (Allowlist post patterns, presence peer patterns), fills the collection to its documented maximum with the worst source the screen accepts AT the bound (derive it from MAX_AMBIGUITY, e.g. '[ab]?'.repeat(log2(MAX_AMBIGUITY))) and asserts one match call against a MAX_MATCH_INPUT-length adversarial input stays under a stated wall-clock budget. Derive the pattern from the constants so raising MAX_AMBIGUITY or the count cap re-grades automatically.

summary: `live_push.mention_filter: true` combined with `live_push.enabled: false` loads cleanly and does nothing. This is the same class the module deliberately fails on elsewhere — `permissions.skip_permissions: true` is rejected because "nothing in core or any plugin reads it", and unknown keys are rejected because they would "leave the operator with a bridge that quietly does nothing".
failure: parseConfig({identity:{handle:'h'}, topics:['t'], live_push:{enabled:false, mention_filter:true}}) succeeds. mentionFilter is read at exactly one place, transport/push-loop.ts:61, reached only from stdio-bridge.ts:115 inside `if (cfg.live_push.enabled)`. An operator who set mention_filter to stop being flooded gets no filtering AND no error. The inverse asymmetry compounds it: the superRefine at line 241 DOES reject a non-mentionable handle whenever mention_filter is true even with enabled:false, so the same dead flag is enforced strictly in one direction and ignored in the other.
remediation: Add a superRefine issue on path ['live_push','mention_filter'] when `mention_filter && !enabled` — 'live_push.mention_filter only applies to the live push path; set live_push.enabled: true or remove mention_filter' — and gate the existing mentionable-handle check on `enabled` too, so the two rules agree about when the flag is live.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a knob that is only read under another knob" with a table of [dependent flag, its enabling flag] pairs (live_push.mention_filter -> live_push.enabled; presence.heartbeat_ms/ttl_ms/topic -> presence.enabled) asserting that setting the dependent while the enabler is false is either a load error or provably has an effect. A row per pair means the next conditional knob is graded when it lands, instead of one fixed case for mention_filter.

summary: The Allowlist class docstring asserts "A reply always targets the inbound topic, which is subscribed (thus in the explicit list) and therefore already allowed." `parley_reply` takes a caller-supplied `topic` argument and is gated by the POST/FETCH set, which includes post_topics pattern matches — so a reply can target a topic that was never subscribed.
failure: transport/tools.ts registers 'parley_reply' with its own `topic` input schema and routes it through the shared doPost -> `deps.allow.assert(topicStr)` (tools.ts:152), i.e. the pattern-widened set. With `post_topics: ['ctx-.*']` and `topics: ['ctx-a']`, parley_reply({topic:'ctx-elsewhere', ...}) is accepted. Since the sentence sits two lines under "Inbound is untrusted", a reader concludes that a prompt-injected instruction to reply elsewhere is structurally impossible; in fact it is bounded only by the post set. No privilege escape (assert still runs) — the claim is what is false, and it is false in the module that defines the boundary.
remediation: Restate it as the mechanism actually in force: a reply is gated by the same post/fetch set as parley_post, so it can reach any explicit topic or post_topics match and nothing else. Per CLAUDE.md the reasoning belongs in the commit message, not in expanded prose here.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "every write entry point is gated by allow.assert and by nothing weaker" so the doc cannot drift again: a parameterized test over the registered write tools (parley_post, parley_reply, and any future one, enumerated from the server's registered tool names rather than a hand list) asserting each rejects a topic outside the post set with TopicNotAllowedError and each ACCEPTS a post_topics-pattern topic that is not in `topics` — the second half is what makes the docstring's claim measurable instead of prose.

summary: `retainFreshest` evicts by Map insertion (message arrival) order, not by beat freshness, so a live long-lived instance is dropped by short-lived siblings of the same handle that beat after it — and the handle then reports `online: false`.
failure: Reproduced with a probe test (deleted). Page for handle `claude-a`, ascending cursor: [heartbeat at=now-60s inst-long ctx-long], then 8 short sessions each posting hello+goodbye (`short-0`..`short-7`, at=now-50s..now-40s). `computeRoster(msgs, now, {ttlMs: 1_800_000, sinceMs: 600_000})[0]` → `{online: false, topics: ['ctx-short']}`. Expected `online: true` and `topics` containing `ctx-long`: the long-lived session beat 60 s ago, well inside a 30-min TTL. `parley_list_users` therefore hides a reachable hand-off partner entirely under `online_only: true`, and drops its topics from the roster otherwise. `instance_id` defaults to the handle and agents are explicitly ephemeral sessions, so this needs no attacker — a handle whose sessions churn faster than its heartbeat reproduces it.
remediation: Make eviction pick the record with the smallest `at` among the tracked instances (decode already rejects any `at` beyond `nowMs + MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS`, so `at` is bounded enough to order on), or preferentially evict `goodbye`/TTL-stale instances before any live one. Then correct the JSDoc, which currently promises exactly the protection the code does not deliver: "the evicted instance is the stalest one rather than a long-lived peer a flood of fresh instanceIds pushed out".
testUpgrade: Parameterize over the POSITION of the surviving instance's last beat within the page — first / middle / last — crossed with the sibling kind (`heartbeat`, `goodbye`) and sibling count (`MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES`, ×2, ×4). Assert in every cell that a handle with at least one non-`goodbye` beat inside `ttlMs` comes back `online: true` and carries that instance's topics. The existing `retains the instances still beating and evicts the stalest` case pins only the `last` column and so cannot fail on this class.

summary: Deleting `insts.delete(rec.instanceId)` from `retainFreshest` — the entire LRU-refresh mechanism — leaves the whole 1885-test suite green.
failure: Mutation applied to packages/bridge-core/src/engine/presence.ts (`insts.delete(rec.instanceId); insts.set(...)` → `insts.set(...)`), then `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core`: `Tests 1885 passed (1885)`. The guarding test `retains the instances still beating and evicts the stalest` still passes because `inst-loud` beats AGAIN after the flood, so it is re-inserted at the tail either way — the assertion is satisfied by the final beat, not by the refresh. The one line the test names in its title is unreachable by any assertion.
remediation: Add the column the test is missing (survivor beats BEFORE the flood, as in the finding above) so the refresh line has a case that dies without it — and fix the underlying eviction policy at the same time.
testUpgrade: Table `computeRoster` instance-retention over (survivor beat position ∈ {before, interleaved, after} × sibling count ∈ {N, 2N, 4N} × sibling kind ∈ {heartbeat, goodbye}) and assert both `online` and topic membership per cell. A generator that shuffles beat arrival order relative to `at` would also catch any future retention policy that silently keys on the wrong one of the two.

summary: `teardown` sets `toreDown = true` before doing any work, so a rejecting `plugin.disconnect()` skips `server.close()` forever and every retry of `shutdown()` is a silent no-op.
failure: Reproduced with a probe (deleted): a `BackendPlugin` whose `disconnect()` rejects with `disconnect boom`. `await bridge.shutdown()` rejects, `server.close()` is never invoked (spy count 0), and a second `await bridge.shutdown()` returns immediately without closing. On the shipped `createStdioBridge` root the `StdioServerTransport` keeps stdin resumed, so the process never exits — an operator's SIGINT handler that awaits `shutdown()` hangs instead of exiting. Network backends whose close handshake can reject (Matrix/XMPP/NATS) are exactly the ones that hit this. The `attach` rollback path has the same shape: `teardown().catch(() => {})` swallows it and leaves the server connected.
remediation: Run each teardown step independently (e.g. settle `presence.stop()`, `plugin.disconnect()` and `server.close()` and aggregate failures) rather than short-circuiting on the first rejection, and only latch `toreDown` once every step has been attempted — or leave the latch clearable so a failed teardown is retryable.
testUpgrade: Widen `every startup failure point rolls back identically` into a teardown-failure table: for each teardown step ∈ {presence.stop, plugin.disconnect, server.close} × each entry point ∈ {shutdown(), rollback inside a failed attach}, inject a rejection into that step and assert (a) every OTHER step still ran exactly once, and (b) the process has no live handles afterwards. Today there is no row where `disconnect` itself fails.

summary: `ReadStateStore.load` explicitly rejects non-string cursor values ("a non-string cursor would wedge catch-up"), but `set`/`flush` accept anything and persist it — a missing `nextCursor` silently DELETES the topic's stored read position instead of failing fast.
failure: Reproduced with a probe (deleted). Persist `{ctx: '42'}`, then run `catchUpTopic` against a plugin returning `{messages: []}` with no `nextCursor` (a JS plugin, or a TS plugin returning a value typed away). `set(T, undefined)` → `merged['ctx'] = undefined` → `JSON.stringify` omits the key → on-disk file loses `ctx` entirely. A fresh `ReadStateStore(path).get(T)` returns `undefined` instead of `'42'`, so the next start cold-restarts the topic: it re-drains the recent window and re-warms `seen` from a position the instance had already passed. Silent, permanent, and invisible until a restart. Same path for a numeric cursor: it survives in memory (`get` hands a number back as a `since`) and is discarded by `load` on the next boot.
remediation: Validate in `set` with the same predicate `load` uses — throw a `TypeError` naming the topic and the offending value when `cursor` is not a non-empty string — so a nonconformant plugin fails loudly on the first page instead of quietly resetting read-state. The `this.state[topic]!` non-null assertion in `flush` is what hides it today.
testUpgrade: Add a `nextCursor` shape dimension to `packages/bridge-core/src/testing/nonconformant.ts` (missing, `null`, numeric, empty string) and run the existing catch-up/read-state driver table across it, asserting in every cell that the previously persisted cursor is either unchanged or replaced by a valid string — never deleted. A round-trip property test over `set(t, v)` for arbitrary `v` would also catch the next value type that slips through.

summary: The comment on `this.pending.clear()` states "keep a failed write's topics pending, so that the next flush retries them", but moving the clear ABOVE the write (destroying exactly that behaviour) leaves the suite green.
failure: Mutation: hoist `this.pending.clear()` to before `writeFileSync`/`renameSync` in `flush`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` → `Tests 1885 passed (1885)`. The `a failed atomic write leaves no debris` table asserts only that `set()` throws and no `.tmp` file survives; nothing observes that the failed topic is re-attempted. With the mutation, a topic whose flush failed is never written again — a later successful flush for a different topic silently publishes stale disk state for the first.
remediation: Keep the current ordering and add the missing observation: make the write fail once, then succeed, and assert the first topic's cursor appears on disk.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing `a failed atomic write leaves no debris` table with a `then recovers` column: for each failure mode, make the write fail for the first N attempts and succeed on N+1, then assert the on-disk file contains EVERY topic set during the failing window. Parameterize over N ∈ {1, 2} and over whether the retry `set` targets the same topic or a different one.

summary: The nap's deadline clamp `sleep(Math.min(pollIntervalMs, remaining))` can be replaced by `sleep(pollIntervalMs)` with the whole suite still green — nothing pins that the long poll respects its own `blockMs` budget when the poll cadence is coarser than the remaining budget.
failure: Mutation: `await sleep(Math.min(opts.pollIntervalMs, Math.max(0, deadline - now())))` → `await sleep(opts.pollIntervalMs)`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` → `Tests 1885 passed (1885)`. Every existing case uses `blockMs` an exact multiple of `pollIntervalMs` (1000/250, 1000/400), where the two expressions coincide. With the mutation and the shipped default `block_poll_interval_ms: 250`, a `parley_fetch_recent` with `block_ms: 10` on an empty topic returns after ~250 ms and issues one extra backend query — the `block_ms` contract ("hold up to this long") is exceeded and the caller's budget is not a bound.
remediation: Keep the clamp; add a case whose budget is NOT a multiple of the cadence.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the deadline behaviour over (blockMs, pollIntervalMs) pairs including pollIntervalMs > blockMs (e.g. 10/250), non-multiples (e.g. 900/250, 1/1000) and the multiple case, asserting BOTH the virtual-clock time at resolution is <= blockMs and the exact `fetchRecent` call count. The existing `an un-aborted budget queries once per poll interval and once at the deadline` case only covers the multiple column.

summary: `SeenSet`'s shipped defaults (`maxPerTopic = 4096`, `maxTopics = 256`) are documented in prose but asserted nowhere — every test injects its own values, so the production dedup window can be changed silently.
failure: Mutation: `private readonly maxTopics = 256` → `= 2`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` → `Tests 1885 passed (1885)`. `buildBridge` constructs `new SeenSet()` with no arguments, so in production this would collapse the LRU to two topics: a three-topic bridge would evict a hot topic's dedup bucket on every cross-topic message and re-emit already-delivered `<channel>` events after each catch-up/live overlap. Nothing in the suite observes the default-constructed instance's capacity.
remediation: Assert the defaults where the prose states them — construct a default `SeenSet`, write `maxPerTopic + 1` ids to one topic and touch `maxTopics + 1` topics, and pin the eviction boundary against the exported constants (which should be exported rather than inline literals).
testUpgrade: Fold the seen-set defaults into `packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts`, which already grades documented inclusive bounds three cells each (at / one inside / one outside) from the constant rather than a literal. The same row is missing for `MAX_FETCH_LIMIT` and `PRESENCE_FETCH_LIMIT` in transport/tools.ts — add all of them so a future constant inherits the grading.

summary: `hostnameOf`'s `.toLowerCase()` — the case-normalisation the DNS-rebinding gate depends on — can be deleted with the suite still green.
failure: Mutation: `return hostname.toLowerCase();` → `return hostname;`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` → `Tests 1885 passed (1885)`. With the mutation a request carrying `Host: LocalHost:8080` (legal and common from browsers and proxies) gets a 403 from a loopback-default deployment, and an operator's `allowedHosts: ['Parley.Example']` never matches an incoming lowercase `Host`. The host-gate tests only ever send already-lowercase values.
remediation: Keep the normalisation and add mixed-case rows on both sides of the comparison (configured value and incoming header).
testUpgrade: Parameterize the host/origin gate over a table of header spellings — mixed case, bracketed IPv6 with and without port, explicit port, missing header, `Origin: null`, trailing dot, and a suffix-attack host such as `127.0.0.1.evil.com` — crossed with configured-allowlist spellings, asserting allow/deny per cell. One table replaces the ad-hoc cases and covers the next normalisation rule too.

summary: `computeRoster`'s entire contract JSDoc (lines 213-235) is immediately followed by a second JSDoc block for `emitterOf`, so it attaches to nothing; `computeRoster` itself (line 277) ships with no doc comment at all.
failure: Read the file: the block beginning `Reconstruct the reachability roster from the presence topic's messages (DESIGN §7)` ends at line 235, line 236 opens a new `/**` documenting `emitterOf`, and `function emitterOf` is declared at 242. `export function computeRoster` at 277 has no preceding comment. Hovering `computeRoster` in an editor, or generating API docs, yields no documentation for the function whose contract that block describes — including the per-instance liveness rule and the `MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES` bound. Worse, the orphaned block is precisely where the false claim in the finding above lives, so a reader who does find it is misled about behaviour that a reader of `computeRoster` never sees.
remediation: Move the block down to sit directly above `export function computeRoster`, and trim it to the risk it warns a future developer off (per CLAUDE.md), pushing the rationale into the commit message.
testUpgrade: Extend `packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts` with a check that no exported function in the package is preceded by a doc-less declaration when a JSDoc block exists earlier in the file with no declaration between it and the next JSDoc — i.e. flag any JSDoc block whose next non-blank line is another `/**`. That is a mechanical rule covering every orphaned block, not just this one.

summary: `parley_list_users`'s `topic` parameter says "Omit for all configured topics; the default scope is the configured topics", but the unscoped path is bidirectional reachability over the POST/FETCH set, which includes pattern-allowed topics that are not configured.
failure: Traced through `filterReachable` (engine/presence.ts:391-401) with `topics: ['ctx']`, `post_topics: ['ops-.*']`. A peer advertising only `topics: ['ops-1']` is included unscoped, because `opts.canPostTo('ops-1')` (`allow.has`) matches the pattern — yet `ops-1` is not a configured topic. The tool's own main description states the correct rule ("anyone you can post to, or who can post to a topic you subscribe to"); the field description contradicts it, and both ship to the model in the tool list. An agent that trusts the field description will not expect pattern-reachable peers in the default roster.
remediation: Restate the field as "Omit for everyone you share a channel with in either direction (see above); pass a topic to scope to peers on that topic." Same class applies to `describeAllowed`, which advertises `any topic fully matching regex …` without noting the presence topic is reserved and will still be refused.
testUpgrade: Add a description-vs-behaviour table: for each tool, extract the registered description text and assert the behavioural claims it makes are exercised by a paired assertion — concretely, a case with `post_topics` set that asserts a peer reachable ONLY via a pattern appears in the unscoped roster, and a case asserting the reserved presence topic is refused by `parley_post`/`parley_fetch_recent` despite matching an advertised `.*` pattern.

summary: `decodePresence` DROPS over-long topic strings with the stated reason that truncating "would fabricate a different topic name", yet truncates over-long `handle` and `instanceId` with `slice()` — fabricating a different identity and silently merging distinct peers/instances into one roster key.
failure: Traced: `r.handle.slice(0, MAX_HANDLE_LEN)` (line 209) and `r.instanceId.slice(0, MAX_INSTANCE_ID_LEN)` (line 204). Two peers whose handles share a 128-character prefix and differ only after it collapse into a single `RosterEntry`, unioning their topics and `postTopics` and reporting one as online when only the other is. The same slice means two distinct instances of one handle sharing a 128-char `instanceId` prefix occupy one slot, so one's `goodbye` reaps the other. The file states the correct policy 17 lines earlier for topics and then does the opposite for the two fields that are actually used as MAP KEYS, where a collision is more consequential than for a list element.
remediation: Drop the record (or drop just the offending field, falling back to `senderHandle` / the anonymous-instance sentinel) when `handle`/`instanceId` exceeds its cap, matching the policy the file already states for topics.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a decode policy table over every capped string field (`topics[]`, `postTopics[]`, `handle`, `instanceId`) × {at the cap, one over, far over}, asserting the SAME policy in every cell — and add a roster-level case proving two records differing only past the cap yield two distinct entries rather than one merged one.

summary: `trustProxy: true` is accepted by the public option and turns `req.ip` into an attacker-controlled header value, so every rate limiter on the built-in front door — including the 10/15min brute-force gate on the owner passphrase — becomes unlimited. The JSDoc warns only about the *default* (`false`) being too strict and never that `true`, the value Express operators reach for first, is the one that removes the protection entirely.
failure: Boot `createOAuthRemoteApp({ issuerUrl, verifyOwner, trustProxy: true })` behind the documented reverse-proxy topology (proxy appends the real client IP, so the chain is `<spoofed>, <realIP>`). 25 consecutive POSTs to `/parley/consent` with a rotating leading `X-Forwarded-For` all return 403 (wrong passphrase) — zero 429s. The identical probe under the documented `trustProxy: 'loopback'` returns 429 from request 11 onward. Measured statuses: true -> [403 x25]; 'loopback' -> [403 x10, 429 x15]. Consequence: unbounded online guessing of the single owner secret that authorizes the whole bridge, plus unbounded /token, /register, /revoke and /authorize.
remediation: Reject a permissive value at the factory instead of forwarding it: in `createOAuthRemoteApp`, throw when `oauth.trustProxy === true` (and when it is the string `'*'`/`0.0.0.0/0`-style catch-alls), naming the safe alternatives ('loopback', a hop count, or a concrete CIDR) the way `assertOptionsMatchMode` already fails fast on stray options. Keep `false` as the default. express-rate-limit already logs ERR_ERL_PERMISSIVE_TRUST_PROXY here, which is evidence the value is known-dangerous and evidence that a log line is not a control.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a `trust proxy` value under which two different X-Forwarded-For chains do NOT share a bucket even though they come from the same real client'. Widen the existing `TOPOLOGIES` table in remote.test.ts (currently only `false` and `'loopback'`) into a table of `{ trustProxy, accepted: boolean, spoofable: boolean }` rows covering `true`, `'*'`, `2` (hop count), `'loopback'`, `false`, `'203.0.113.0/24'`; for accepted rows drive `LIMITED_ROUTES` with a *two-element* XFF chain `'<rotating>, <fixed real ip>'` (the current rows send a single value, which cannot distinguish `true` from `'loopback'` at all) and assert the limiter still reaches 429; for refused rows assert the factory throws naming the option. That row shape also catches any future proxy option added to `OAuthRemoteOptions`.

summary: The comment at line 9 and the operator-facing error text at line 53 both assert that the built-in OAuth front door 'refuses a non-https issuer whatever its host'. That is false. The MCP SDK's `checkIssuerUrl` (node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/server/auth/router.js:15) exempts exactly `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` — the same two hosts this module's own LOOPBACK_HOSTS allows. The real reason `[::1]` must stay out is that the SDK's exemption list omits it, not that the SDK is host-blind.
failure: `createOAuthRemoteApp({ issuerUrl: new URL('http://localhost:PORT'), verifyOwner })` boots and serves (verified by direct execution, and by the passing BASE_URL_SHAPES row `http://localhost:PORT/ -> boots`), which the documented rule says is impossible. An operator who reads the shipped error message 'the built-in OAuth front door refuses a non-https issuer whatever its host' concludes their `http://127.0.0.1` dev setup is also unsupported and either adds TLS they do not need or deletes the loopback exemption; a maintainer who believes it will not realise that adding `[::1]` to LOOPBACK_HOSTS breaks only the builtin door.
remediation: State the actual rule in both places: the SDK's issuer exemption covers only `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`, so a base URL this guard accepts must be drawn from the same set for it to boot on both front doors. Derive LOOPBACK_HOSTS from that fact in one place rather than restating a mechanism.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a comment/error message that names a mechanism in a dependency'. Add a table in invariants.test.ts pairing every host in LOOPBACK_HOSTS plus `[::1]` with the SDK's own `checkIssuerUrl` — i.e. `it.each(HOSTS)` asserting that `assertPublicBaseUrl` accepting `http://<host>` implies `mcpAuthRouter({issuerUrl: new URL('http://<host>')})` constructs without throwing, and that a rejected host is rejected by our message before the SDK's. That fails the moment the SDK changes its exemption set or someone widens ours, and it makes the rationale executable instead of prose. Existing BASE_URL_SHAPES rows assert the outcome but nothing asserts the stated cause.

summary: `hardenErrorSurface(remote.app)` in the delegated-OIDC front door is covered by nothing. The 96-cell error-surface matrix boots only `createOAuthRemoteApp`; `createOidcRemoteApp` never appears in error-surface.test.ts. The call is a security control whose removal is invisible to the gate that decides whether a change lands.
failure: Mutation: replace `hardenErrorSurface(remote.app);` with `void hardenErrorSurface;` in oidc-remote.ts. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-core` -> `Test Files 39 passed (39)`, 0 failures. With the call removed and NODE_ENV unset (the state the shipped run command in examples/self-host-remote/README.md leaves it in), the app's `env` is 'development' and any framework error reaching Express's default handler renders `err.stack` — absolute install paths and frame list — into the response body. Today that path needs a valid bearer (because `protect` runs before `express.json()` on /mcp), but any route a future `configureApp` mounts ahead of `protect`, or any unauthenticated route added to the metadata router, reopens it unguarded.
remediation: Parameterize the error-surface suite over both factories rather than adding a second bespoke file, so a third front door inherits the coverage.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a hardening step applied per-factory, verified for only one factory'. Lift the FACTORIES table already used by teardown.test.ts (which does parameterize over both remote-app factories) into a shared fixture and drive error-surface.test.ts's BOOT_ENVS x ROUTES x TRIGGERS matrix from it, with each factory contributing its own route list. Add one route per factory that is mounted *before* `protect` and throws, so the assertion has a negative control in both modes. This also catches the next control that gets applied in `remote.ts` but forgotten in `oidc-remote.ts`.

summary: The docblock says 'Keep BOTH halves of this', but only one half is measured. Deleting `app.use(terminalErrorHandler)` leaves the entire suite green, because with `env` pinned to 'production' Express's own finalhandler already emits a stackless status phrase, already sets `err.status`, and already calls console.error — satisfying every assertion in the 'really does reach the terminal handler' negative control (status 413, no 'PayloadTooLargeError', logged). The `statusOf` 400–599 clamp is likewise unmeasured.
failure: Mutation A: delete `app.use(terminalErrorHandler);` -> `Test Files 39 passed (39)`. Mutation B: weaken `statusOf`'s range check from `typeof claimed !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(claimed) || claimed < 400 || claimed > 599` to `typeof claimed !== 'number'` -> `Test Files 39 passed (39)`; an error carrying `status: 200` or `status: 1.5` is then reflected as the response status. Control: deleting `app.set('env','production')` DOES fail 2 tests, so the suite discriminates one half and not the other. Either the handler is redundant (and is dead weight on the request path) or it is load-bearing and ships unverified.
remediation: Decide which. If it stays, pin what only it does: `content-type: text/plain`, the exact `<status> <phrase>` body, the `[parley]` log prefix, and the clamp of an out-of-range `err.status`. If it does not, delete it and let the env pin carry the docblock's claim alone.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a defence whose stated contribution is already delivered by something else in the chain'. Add a table over injected error shapes — `{status:200}`, `{status:999}`, `{status:1.5}`, `{statusCode:413}`, `{}`, a string throw, an error thrown after `res.writeHead` (headersSent path) — mounted via a route registered before the terminal handler, asserting response status, `content-type`, and exact body for each row. Then re-run the mutation: each row must fail with the handler removed. Generalise it as 'for every element of hardenErrorSurface, removing it alone turns at least one row red' so a third half added later inherits the requirement.

summary: `assertPublicBaseUrl` checks 'https, or a loopback host' but never checks that the scheme is http/https at all. Any scheme on `localhost`/`127.0.0.1` passes, and for a non-special scheme `URL.origin` is the string 'null', so `canonicalResourceId`'s `resource.origin !== base.origin` cross-origin guard degenerates to `'null' !== 'null'` and cannot fire either. The guard's own docblock says it exists so a server cannot 'boot healthy and then 401 every token'.
failure: `createOAuthRemoteApp(plugin, cfg, { issuerUrl: new URL('htp://localhost:8080'), verifyOwner })` — a one-character operator typo — boots and reports `resource = htp://localhost:8080/mcp`. Verified by direct execution; `foo://127.0.0.1:8080` and `ws://localhost:8080` boot identically. Every token is then minted with an audience no client can dereference, the advertised RFC 9728 resource identifier names a scheme nothing speaks, and nothing at boot says so. The SDK's own `checkIssuerUrl` does not catch it either (same 'https OR loopback host' shape).
remediation: Add an explicit scheme check to `assertPublicBaseUrl`: `url.protocol` must be `https:`, or `http:` on a loopback host; anything else is refused by name. Same for `assertTrustRootUrl`, which has the identical shape and would accept `htp://localhost/jwks` as a JWKS trust root.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a URL component the guard does not constrain'. Extend BASE_URL_SHAPES in invariants.test.ts with a scheme axis — `htp://localhost:PORT`, `foo://127.0.0.1:PORT`, `ws://localhost:PORT`, `file://localhost/`, `https://localhost:PORT` — each with an explicit boots/refuses outcome, and mirror the same rows onto `assertTrustRootUrl` in the trust-root ROWS table. Better still, drive it from a generator over `{scheme} x {host} x {path,query,fragment,userinfo}` and assert the invariant 'accepted implies `new URL(mcpPath, base).protocol` is http: or https: and `base.origin !== "null"`', which catches components nobody enumerated.

summary: `exchangeAuthorizationCode` compares `redirectUri !== rec.redirectUri` unconditionally. When a client with exactly one registered redirect URI omits `redirect_uri` from BOTH the authorization request and the token request — explicitly legal under RFC 6749 §4.1.3 / OAuth 2.1 §4.1.3, which make it REQUIRED at /token only *if* it was present at /authorize — the SDK defaults `rec.redirectUri` to `client.redirect_uris[0]` at /authorize and then passes `undefined` at /token, so the exchange always fails.
failure: DCR a client with a single `redirect_uris` entry; GET /authorize with `client_id`, `response_type=code`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256` and no `redirect_uri`; approve consent; POST /token with `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code`, `code_verifier` and no `redirect_uri` -> HTTP 400 `invalid_grant` 'authorization grant is invalid or expired'. The owner has already given consent and burned the code, so the only diagnostic is a generic invalid_grant and the flow is unrecoverable without re-consenting. Traced through authorize.js:92 (`redirect_uri = client.redirect_uris[0]`) and token.js (`redirect_uri` optional).
remediation: Record on the CodeRecord whether the client actually supplied `redirect_uri` at /authorize (the provider can see the difference only if the SDK forwards it, so either carry a flag or compare `redirectUri ?? rec.redirectUri`), and require the exact match only when it was supplied. Alternatively, refuse the /authorize request outright when `redirect_uri` is absent, so the client learns at the first hop instead of after the owner has consented — but do not leave the strictness silently at the last hop.
testUpgrade: The class is 'a request shape the spec permits that this AS refuses, discovered only after consent is spent'. Turn the existing single case 'rejects a token exchange that omits redirect_uri' into a table over `{ suppliedAtAuthorize, suppliedAtToken, matches }` — all four combinations plus a mismatching value — with the expected outcome for each drawn from the RFC, and assert the failing rows fail *before* the pending consent is consumed where the spec allows an early refusal. Same table shape should cover `resource` (present/absent at each hop), which has the same two-hop optionality.

summary: Nothing grades that `parley_meta.store_id` is read BACK rather than re-minted, so the entire justification of the `<storeId>.<rowid>` cursor design — that a cursor stays honourable across a bridge restart against the same file — is uncovered. test/cursor-replay.test.ts grades only the REPLAY arm across a reconnect (reset / backup-restore); every case asserting the HONOURED arm runs on one live connection where the in-memory storeId is trivially stable.
failure: Mutation: in `readOrMintStoreId`, replace `return row.value;` with `return randomBytes(8).toString('hex');` (INSERT OR IGNORE and the row===undefined guard intact). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite` -> 341/341 PASS. Probe of the resulting shipped behaviour: connect(db_path=P); post m0,m1,m2; tail = fetchRecent({topic}).nextCursor; disconnect(); new SqlitePlugin().connect(db_path=P); fetchRecent({topic, since: tail}) returns ['m0','m1','m2'] instead of []. In production that is: every bridge restart treats core's persisted read-state as foreign and replays the whole topic window, and core's SeenSet is in-memory, so a Code session re-emits the replayed window as <channel> events on every start.
remediation: No src change needed — the code is correct today; add the missing guard. Introduce a restart-generation case in test/cursor-replay.test.ts that reconnects to the SAME file and asserts the pre-disconnect cursor is still exclusive and that the store id is byte-identical across the reconnect.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a cursor survives a generation boundary that did NOT change the store' with a table over (transition) x (cursor position): transitions = [same-file reconnect, reconnect after more posts, reconnect after a retention prune, reconnect after a clean close/WAL checkpoint]; positions = [0, first row, mid, tail, tail-after-more-rows]. Each row asserts (a) drained contents equal exactly the rows after the cursor and (b) storeIdOf(p) is identical before and after. Run it alongside the existing UNHONOURABLE_CURSORS table so both arms — replay for a foreign store, exclusivity for the same store — are pinned across a reconnect, not only within one connection. The existing 'a store restored from an older backup' case is too narrow: it expects a replay either way, so it passes under the mutation.

summary: The poll loop wraps `handler(rowToMessage(row, storeId))` in a try/catch so a throwing consumer cannot be mistaken for a database failure. No test in the package ever registers a handler that throws, so the guard counts as coverage while being ungraded.
failure: Mutation: delete the try/catch, leaving a bare `handler(rowToMessage(row, storeId));`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite` -> 342/342 PASS. With the guard gone, one throwing handler invocation (core's push loop emitting into a closed stdio transport, e.g. EPIPE) falls into the loop's DB-error catch, is classified `unavailable`, prints a misleading `parley-sqlite: poll error on topic "ctx"`, and after 10 such ticks drives the topic to state 'degraded' with a backoff toward 30 s — a consumer bug reported to the operator as a store outage, throttling live push.
remediation: No src change needed. Add a case to test/background-jobs.test.ts subscribing a handler that throws on the first N messages, asserting later messages still arrive, no `poll error` line is written, and subscriptionHealth(T)[0] stays state 'live' with consecutiveFailures 0.
testUpgrade: Add a second dimension to the existing ERROR_CASES decision table — WHO threw. Parameterize source = ['select statement', 'handler'] x the existing SQLITE_*/unclassified rows, asserting that only the 'select statement' source may move `state` off 'live' or emit a diagnostic. That also catches the inverse regression (a widened guard that swallows real DB errors).

summary: The README justifies throwing on an unparseable cursor by claiming it costs one page: 'absorbing it would wedge the topic's catch-up forever instead of costing one page.' Rejecting it actually costs the whole bridge: resumeAfter throws, catchUpAll rethrows out of buildBridge, and cli.ts's main().catch exits 1 — permanently, on every subsequent start, until an operator deletes read-state.
failure: Reproduced with the shipped dist/cli.js: config with state_path pointing at {"ctx":"s123_456"} (a Matrix-shaped cursor left behind by repointing an instance from parley-matrix to parley-sqlite under the default instance_id) -> stderr 'parley-sqlite: fatal: Error: catch-up failed on topic "ctx" ... malformed cursor', EXIT=1, identical on retry. The doc also hides an inconsistency: a foreign NUMERIC cursor ('123456789', a NATS/Telegram id) self-heals by replaying, while a foreign non-numeric one is a hard startup failure.
remediation: Restate the cost honestly in README.md and in the resumeAfter JSDoc: an unparseable cursor stops the bridge at catch-up-on-start until read-state is cleared (core's error already names the file and the fix). Keeping the fail-fast behaviour is defensible; describing it as 'one page' is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a documented failure cost matches the observed blast radius' with a table in src/cli.test.ts over (bad persisted state) x (expected blast radius): [malformed cursor -> non-zero exit + message naming state_path], [foreign numeric cursor -> bridge up + topic replayed], [foreign storeId cursor -> bridge up + replayed], [own cursor above high water -> bridge up + replayed]. Each row asserts the process verdict, so a change to either the behaviour or the prose that desynchronizes them turns red.

summary: README: 'test/multi-process.test.ts covers the pragmas themselves: each one is asserted through an observable consequence (`PRAGMA` read-back, the -wal sidecar appearing on disk, a contended write retrying ...)'. That file's PRAGMAS block reads no pragma back — it only asserts the README mentions each pragma name and consequence. The read-back lives in test/driver-parity.test.ts, whose own comment says so.
failure: multi-process.test.ts lines 52-82: the per-pragma `it` bodies are `expect(README).toContain(p.name)` / `expect(README).toMatch(p.consequence)`. A reader following the README to verify the pragma claim lands on a doc-string check and concludes pragma VALUES are graded there when they are not; if driver-parity.test.ts were deleted, the README would still point at a file grading nothing about pragma values.
remediation: Point the sentence at test/driver-parity.test.ts for the read-back, and describe multi-process.test.ts as covering the -wal sidecar, the contended write, the DDL-drift comparison and the README-documentation check.
testUpgrade: Add a README-claim table mapping each named test file to a regex its content must match (multi-process.test.ts -> /-wal|busy_timeout|byte-identical DDL/, driver-parity.test.ts -> /PRAGMA \$\{p\.name\}/), so a claim naming the wrong file fails instead of rotting. This is the same ratchet as the finding above, applied to file attribution rather than blast radius.

summary: subscribe() keys this.health by topic and overwrites unconditionally, but starts an independent poll loop on every call. Two subscriptions to one topic run two loops while subscriptionHealth() reports one entry — contradicting the invariant test/lifecycle.test.ts names ('subscriptionHealth never reports a loop that cannot deliver'). The plugin also silently double-delivers rather than failing fast on a call it cannot represent, unlike connect(), which refuses to run twice.
failure: Probe: connect(poll_interval_ms=10); subscribe('ctx', a); subscribe('ctx', b); post('ctx','x') -> observed handlerA=['x'] handlerB=['x'] health=[{"topic":"ctx","state":"live","consecutiveFailures":0}] — one health record for two live loops. If the first loop later takes 10 consecutive fatal errors it sets state 'stopped' on an object no longer in the map, so a supervisor polling subscriptionHealth() reads 'live' for a handler that has permanently stopped receiving. Core never subscribes twice today, so this is embedder-facing rather than a shipped outage.
remediation: Either reject a duplicate subscribe(topic) with a named error (fail-fast, matching connect()'s posture), or key health per subscription and have subscriptionHealth(topic) return one record per loop.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'every started loop is represented in subscriptionHealth' with a parameterized case over subscription counts [1, 2, 3] on the same topic and on distinct topics: assert subscriptionHealth().length equals the number of loops that can deliver, and that after breaking the Nth loop's select the report shows a non-'live' entry. The same table catches the inverse (a loop torn down but still reported).

summary: `retention_days` can be made a complete no-op and all 304 bridge-redis tests stay green. Every retention case grades only the negative direction ("history is KEPT"); nothing anywhere asserts that a single entry is ever trimmed, so the knob's one observable effect is uncovered while the README and DESIGN §11 both promise it.
failure: Mutation: replace the `this.retentionDays !== undefined ?` guard on the `XADD ... TRIM {MINID ~}` option with `false` (i.e. never send a trim). `PARLEY_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6399 npx vitest run --root . packages/bridge-redis` → `Test Files 9 passed (9) / Tests 304 passed (304)`. A shipped bridge configured `retention_days: 30` would then retain every message forever — unbounded Redis memory growth on the exact backends whose store Parley owns — with no test, no error and no log line. The nearest cases (live-failure-modes.test.ts:90 `%s keeps every posted message`, :164 `every accepted %s round-trips post → fetchRecent`) pass a retention window and assert nothing was deleted, which the mutant satisfies perfectly.
remediation: Add a positive-direction retention case. Verified feasible against a real server: seed ~200 entries at explicit ids 30 days in the past via an independent writer (`xAdd(key, `${old+i}-0`, …)`), connect the plugin with `retention_days: 1`, issue one `post`, then assert `XLEN` collapsed to the fresh entry (measured: 200 old → 1 remaining, 1000 old → 1 remaining, 5 old → 6 remaining because `~` trims whole nodes).
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a config knob whose only effect is on backend state is graded solely by its negative direction": add a table over the knob's *effect*, parameterized by (retention_days, seeded age, seeded volume) — e.g. rows [{days:1, ageDays:30, n:200, expect:'trimmed'}, {days:30, ageDays:1, n:200, expect:'kept'}, {days:1, ageDays:30, n:5, expect:'kept — approximate trim, node-granular'}] — asserting XLEN/fetchRecent contents in both directions from one generator. The third row also pins the `~` approximation the README claims, which no test currently exercises. Apply the same both-directions rule to every knob in CONFIG_KEYS whose effect is externally observable.

summary: The README, the shipped npm `description`, and the RedisPlugin class JSDoc all state that `fetchRecent` is exclusive on `since` (`XRANGE <key> (since +`). It is not: a cursor sorting past the stream's last generated id silently re-queries the whole recent window with XREVRANGE and returns messages STRICTLY BEFORE `since`, with a regressed `nextCursor`. The sibling backends that do the same thing document it (bridge-sqlite README:31-32, bridge-nats README:33); this one does not.
failure: `fetchRecent({topic, since: '<Date.now()+86400000>-0'})` on a topic holding messages a,b → returns `{messages:[a,b], nextCursor: <cursor of b>}`, i.e. two messages older than the cursor the caller asked to read strictly after, and a cursor lower than the one supplied. Pinned by live-failure-modes.test.ts:515 and core-catchup.test.ts:86 (`resolves.toBe(2)`), so the behaviour is deliberate — only the docs are wrong. An operator reading the README's mapping table cannot predict a whole-window replay into a live session, and `package.json`'s "XRANGE for exclusive-since catch-up" ships that claim to npm.
remediation: Add a short README paragraph (mirroring bridge-sqlite's) stating that a cursor above the stream's high-water mark — a re-created dataset, a repointed `url`, a changed `key_prefix`, an evicted key — is treated as unset, so catch-up self-heals by replaying the most recent `limit` entries and returning a lower `nextCursor`. Soften the `fetchRecent` row in the mapping table and the class JSDoc accordingly.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a behaviour tested in code but absent from the package's own prose": extend readme.test.ts with a table mapping each named plugin behaviour to a required README phrase — rows for the past-the-tail heal, the labelled-refusal path, the live-delivery-STOPPED line, the block_ms floor — driven from a single exported list so a behaviour added later must add its row. Widen it to grade `package.json.description` with the same phrases, since that string ships to npm independently.

summary: `blockingRead`'s bare `catch { return []; }` swallows permanent, operator-fixable server refusals on the long-poll path, while the `subscribe` loop classifies the identical refusals via `serverRefusal()` and reports them to stderr. The same NOPERM is loud on one path and invisible on the other.
failure: Reproduced against a live redis:7-alpine with `ACL SETUSER poller on >pw ~* &* +@read +@write +@connection +@keyspace -xread`. `subscribe` → stderr: `parley-redis: live delivery STOPPED for topic 'acl2' … NOPERM … 'xread'`. `fetchRecent({topic, since: <tail>, blockMs: 1500})` → resolves `{messages:[], nextCursor:'1785392750481-0'}` in 8ms, no error, no stderr. Core's fetchRecentBlocking then naps 250ms and retries, so every `parley_fetch_recent` with the default 60s budget opens and burns ~240 doomed Redis connections while reporting a normal empty long-poll. The same silence covers any reader-open failure (maxclients, a proxy accepting TCP then stalling — exactly the state live-failure-modes.test.ts:995 creates and never grades the returned page of).
remediation: In `blockingRead`, run the caught error through `serverRefusal()`; on a permanent refusal (or a repeated reader-open failure) surface it — either by rethrowing so `labelled()` names the plugin/topic/key, or at minimum by emitting the same one-line stderr diagnostic `subscribe` already uses. Keep the `[]` fallback only for teardown and transient socket faults.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "the same backend fault is diagnosed on one delivery path and swallowed on another": parameterize the existing permanent/transient reason table (subscribe-hardening.test.ts:233) over PATH ∈ {subscribe, blocking fetchRecent} as well as REASON, asserting that a permanent reason produces a labelled error or a stderr line on both paths and that a transient one produces neither. Add a live row using an ACL user without `xread` so the class is also covered end-to-end rather than only against the mock.

summary: `entryTimestamp` accepts any string `Date.parse` does not reject and forwards it verbatim, so a foreign writer's `ts` can put a non-ISO-8601 value into `Message.timestamp`, which DESIGN §5 declares is ISO 8601. The function's own JSDoc says a foreign entry must "normalize into a Message that satisfies the DESIGN §5 contract"; it only handles the unparseable case.
failure: `XADD parley:t * sender a content x ts 'Mon Jan 01 2020'` (also `'2020'`, `'12/25/2021'`, `'Tue, 05 Nov 2024 10:00:00 GMT'`) → `fetchRecent` returns `timestamp: "Mon Jan 01 2020"` / `"2020"` / `"12/25/2021"` verbatim (reproduced on a live server). That string reaches core, the `<channel>` event and `parley_list_users` as if it were ISO 8601. Worse, non-ISO `Date.parse` input is implementation-defined, so which of these is accepted can differ between Node versions. The guarding row (live-failure-modes.test.ts:295) only uses a proper ISO string, and every other assertion is `!Number.isNaN(Date.parse(ts))` — which the defect satisfies.
remediation: Re-serialize instead of passing through: `const at = Date.parse(ts); return Number.isNaN(at) ? fromId() : new Date(at).toISOString();`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a field with a declared FORMAT is asserted only for parseability": widen the foreign-entry table with a `ts` axis of parseable-but-non-ISO spellings (RFC 2822, `MM/DD/YYYY`, bare year, `YYYY-MM-DD` without time, an offset form) and assert `m.timestamp === new Date(m.timestamp).toISOString()` for every row rather than `!isNaN(Date.parse(...))`. The same shape assertion belongs in the conformance suite's expectWellFormedMessage so it grades all eleven backends.

summary: subscribe() seeds the `limited`-burst backfill boundary (`lastDelivered`) from `timelineTip()`, an HTTP round-trip AFTER the positioning `/sync` fixed `nextBatch`. Any event that lands in that window is post-subscription (it is newer than nextBatch, so it MUST be delivered) but is treated as already-delivered, so the backward `backfill` stops at it and silently discards it and everything between it and nextBatch.
failure: FakeSynapse, per-topic room, syncCap=3. Post 'seed'; call subscribe(T). Using onRequest, land window-0..window-2 while the timelineTip `/messages?dir=b&limit=1` request is in flight (positioning /sync has already returned). Then land burst-0..burst-9 so the first incremental /sync is `limited`. Handler receives ['burst-0'..'burst-9'] — window-0..2 are NEVER delivered, and limitedEmitted === 1 proves the backfill path ran. Expected all 13 in order. On a real Synapse the same shape is a >100-event burst plus any traffic in the one round-trip between the positioning sync and the tip read; those events never become `<channel>` events for the running session.
remediation: Do not use a separately-read tip as the delivery boundary. Either (a) derive the boundary from the positioning sync itself — e.g. take the tip BEFORE the positioning `/sync` so it can only be at or behind nextBatch (over-including is safe: the `skip` set and the ascending re-delivery order handle overlap, and per-topic rooms cannot leak foreign history), or (b) stop paging backfill at the positioning `next_batch` token rather than at an event id, so the boundary is exactly the subscription position. Keep the shared_room pre-history guard by intersecting with, not replacing, that position.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a live-path recovery boundary established at a different instant than the subscription position'. Parameterize the existing `subscribe recovers a burst larger than the per-sync cap via prev_batch` table (catchup-sync.fake.test.ts) with a new axis WHEN-EVENTS-LAND: {before subscribe, inside the positioning /sync, inside the timelineTip read, after subscribe returns} x {syncCap 1,2,3} x {prevBatchOverlap 0,1,2} x {shared_room true,false}, asserting the handler sees EXACTLY the post-position events, once, ascending. Add a fake hook that lands events before a named request's body is computed (FakeSynapse.onRequest already does this) and record which hook fired, so a row that armed nothing fails instead of grading a different window. The current table only lands events after `await p.subscribe(...)`, so no row can reach this cell.

Reproduced: POST /createRoom body is `{"room_alias_name":"parley_t","preset":"trusted_private_chat","visibility":"private"}` and console.warn emitted zero lines. A junk value is forwarded too: `room_preset: public_chat_lol` produced `{"preset":"public_chat_lol",...}` on the wire (a homeserver 400 at first post, not at load). Add a table over EVERY typed field of MatrixBackendConfig x {a value outside its union/type, a value of the wrong JS type, a value out of range}, driving `new MatrixPlugin().connect(cfg as unknown as BackendConfig)` and asserting it REJECTS (or, where lenience is intended, warns) — never that the value reaches `fake.createRoomBodies` / the request URLs. summary: `sync_timeout_ms` is documented as "Unbounded" and is never validated. `blockingFetch` computes `slice = Math.min(remaining, this.syncTimeoutMs)`; with `sync_timeout_ms: 0` (or negative) the slice is 0, so the waiter timer fires immediately and the park/re-query loop spins for the whole budget, re-running the canonical `/context` + `/messages` catch-up each pass. `pollBoundedSync` has an explicit anti-hot-spin pace guard for exactly this shape; the blocking park and the subscribe loop have none.
failure: backend_config `{ sync_timeout_ms: 0 }`; post a seed, take the tail cursor, then `fetchRecent({ topic, since: tail, blockMs: 500 })`. Reproduced: 218 `/messages` requests issued during that single 500ms call (222 with `sync_timeout_ms: -1`). At the production default `catchup.block_max_ms: 60000` one idle `parley_fetch_recent` becomes roughly 26,000 homeserver requests — self-inflicted rate-limit exhaustion from a single config typo, with no warning at load.
remediation: Validate `sync_timeout_ms` in `connect()` (positive integer; reject 0/negative/NaN, naming the default), and independently floor the park slice — e.g. `Math.min(remaining, Math.max(this.syncTimeoutMs, MIN_SLICE_MS))` — so no config value can turn the wait into a re-query storm. Consider giving the subscribe loop the same pace guard `pollBoundedSync` already carries, so a non-blocking or degenerate `/sync` endpoint cannot hot-spin it either.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a timing knob whose degenerate values collapse a wait into a request storm'. Add a parameterized case over sync_timeout_ms in {0, -1, NaN, 1, 50, 25000} x {blocking fetchRecent with blockMs=500, subscribe loop for 500ms} asserting a REQUEST-RATE ceiling from `fake.messagesRequests.length` / `fake.syncAttempts.length` (e.g. <= blockMs / MIN_SLICE_MS + k) — not just that the call returns. Note the existing sync-deadline.fake.test.ts sweeps sync_timeout_ms only over {1000, 25000, 30000, 60000} and asserts deadlines, never a rate, so no degenerate value is reachable there.

summary: `existingRoom` gates on `isStale(generation)` BEFORE `await this.joinRoom(...)` and then repopulates `this.rooms` after it. The JSDoc claims the gate stops a teardown landing mid-resolve from joining with a cleared token and repopulating `rooms` for the next generation, but a `disconnect()` landing during the awaited join is not covered: the join completes post-teardown and `this.rooms.set(key, ...)` re-adds an entry `disconnect()` just cleared. Compounding it, the cached fast path at line 920 returns the cached room with no staleness check at all.

Harm is bounded (the next `connect()` clears `rooms`, and the token is gone so requests would 401), but the stated guard does not hold and the cached-entry fast path would serve it.
